newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: INSTANT VIEW -Economists' views on RBNZ statement.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW -Economists' views on RBNZ statement.

text.p: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand said on Tuesday in its six-monthly monetary policy statement that some easing in New Zealand monetary policy had been warranted but recent market reaction was "somewhat excessive".
Below is some instant reaction from economists and others:
STEPHEN TOPLIS, CHIEF ECONOMIST WITH BROKERAGE DOYLE PATERSON BROWN

"What the bank is saying is that compared with September, we have had a major easing in monetary conditions, we accept that that is appropriate partly because some of the growth indicators have come in less that we had expected, partly because the inflation band is widened and partly because the government has been reasonably fiscally restrained.

"However, while they accept the fact that a significant easing is appropriate, they think that things might have gone a touch too far short-term and as a consequence have warned the market not to take things any further.
"They did not actually say that they required conditions to be tighter than what they were at the time of the statement. They said their preference would be for things to be marginally tighter."

Looking ahead Toplis said: "The bank, given the part of the economic cycle that we're in, is leaning towards an easing bias over time. However, it's now in a period of significant uncertainty because it's hard to work out the impact of some of the fiscal things."
Toplis said it was difficult to work through the impact of the raising of the minimum wage on inflation, for example.
"You have to accept that we are in a period of high uncertainty and the bank is acknowledging that."
Toplis said market reaction was appropriate.
BANCORP TREASURY SERVICES
Bancorp said in a statement that the announcement had been well anticipated, with all commentators coming around to the view that the market-led easing would be sanctioned.

"In this respect then there are no changes to our view of the New Zealand dollar's future. The only change is that the potential for immediate weakness in the New Zealand dollar is postponed to mid-January."

Bancorp said RBNZ governor Don Brash's words were his main weapon in the fight against inflation, and in that regard Brash's comment that the market's easing had been "somewhat excessive" was inappropriate.
Bancorp said the bank was sanctioning current levels. The bank was concerned about the rapid pace that brought them about, not the extent of the moves.

"The RBNZ should not be surprised to see the move be so quick, after all it has seen this happen before. Also, the easing move has been such a long time coming, the pent up expectations of a move to neutral conditions have been building
ANZ BANKING GROUP
ANZ's economics department said in a statement that while recognising the scope for easier conditions, the RBNZ was guarding against a further significant easing in monetary conditions at this time.

"We believe there will be further scope for easing during the first quarter of 1997 -- particularly if the December quarter CPI (to be released January 17) confirms moderating inflation pressures." No text received
BANK OF NEW ZEALAND TREASURY ECONOMIST PETER JOLLY
"They look to be playing a very cautious hand. They are being their usual cautious selves.
"The bank had told the market that it has got ahead of itself -- by about 50 basis points -- and it's time to take stock."
However, Jolly said the bank had indicated there would be further easings down the road.
"I think the market will continue to discount further easings."
However, it had sounded warnings about risks involving the housing market, the fiscal position and inflationary impact of the higher minimum wage.
Jolly said that the bank had taken a narrow interpretation of the new wider 0-3 percent inflation target and would come down strongly against any rise in inflationary expectations.
-- Wellington Newsroom (64-4-4734746)
